# Project summary and structure

The goal of this project is to make declaration data easy to search, browse and interpret.

- `exposed/` contains the rust application and CLI code that powers the project.
- `frontend/` contains a simple Svelte application

## Worktree policy

- For read-only tasks (investigating, reading, summarizing, or describing code),
  work on the current branch without creating a worktree.
- For tasks that require changing code or other files, use [`worktrunk`](https://worktrunk.dev):
  - `wt switch --create <branch-name> --base main`
- Never modify the primary checkout without explicit permission.

## Exposed coding policy

- Follow with strict detail to the existing style of the application. This includes:
  - Type driven design
  - Domain modelling and parse-not-validate
  - Consistent error handling
  - Service layer abstractions

- Interactions with the database must use `sqlx` macros for compile-time query verification.

- For Rust changes, read and apply the
  [Rust domain development skill](.agents/skills/rust-domain-development/SKILL.md).
- Before implementation, identify the domain states, invariants, and the type
  that owns each rule. Parse external values into those types at boundaries and
  retain typed values internally.
- Use one canonical domain enum for each finite vocabulary. Do not duplicate
  its variants in string allowlists. Use exhaustive matches where behavior
  depends on a variant.
- When a bug exposes duplicated domain rules, remove the duplication rather
  than synchronizing the copies. Trace changes through producers, serialization,
  consumers, and persistence together.

## Financial totals contract

- The backend member summary owns mandatory declared GBP totals across all
  categories, including unknown category IDs. Frontends display those fields
  without recalculation or fallback sums.
- Current-term totals include records registered on or after
  `2024-07-09T00:00:00Z`. Historical totals include all records; undated records
  belong only to historical totals.
- Preserve exact decimal amounts and currencies. Do not convert currencies or
  pass amounts through JavaScript `Number`. Missing GBP amounts and unknown
  currencies make totals incomplete; known foreign currencies are excluded from
  GBP amounts without making totals incomplete.
- Preserve declaration counts and distinguish null amounts from zero. Label
  these as declared amounts, not earnings: declarations can include rates and
  benefits rather than money earned.
- Financial semantic changes require explicit user authorization and a description
  of their effects on included records/categories, currency, registration dates,
  missing values, precision, and labels. UI changes and refactoring must preserve
  these rules.

## Frontend coding policy

- Frontend presentation is largely a prototype. UI edits must preserve the financial contract above.

### UI copy scope

- Add only the visible text needed for the requested interaction or data.
  Do not add unrequested subtitles, helper paragraphs, explanatory labels,
  badges, or repeated context to make a feature feel complete.
- Reuse existing wording. Keep required control labels, accessible names,
  error messages, and the financial wording required above.
- Before committing UI changes, review each added visible string against the
  request. Remove optional copy that the user did not request. A component
  example is not permission to copy its explanatory text into a feature.

| Rule | Enforcement |
| --- | --- |
| Omit unrequested visible UI copy. | Review added strings in the diff against the user's request. This is a judgment check; types and automated tests cannot determine whether copy was requested. |

### Client and server

- Use Node.js 24+. From `frontend`, run `npm ci` and `npm run dev` for local
  development. Production uses `npm run build` followed by `node build`.
- Render initial page data through SvelteKit server loads. Keep Rust API access
  and response parsing in `frontend/src/lib/server` and `+page.server.ts`.
- Keep `EXPOSED_API_ORIGIN` on the server. Browser navigation and data requests
  go through the same-origin SvelteKit application, not directly to the Rust API.
- Pass typed, serializable page models to components. Keep browser APIs and SDK
  initialization in client hooks, event handlers, or `onMount` so SSR stays safe.
- Declare public configuration in `frontend/src/env.ts`. Use `dev` from
  `$app/env` for development-only behavior, including the design-system route.

### PostHog

- Initialize PostHog in `frontend/src/hooks.client.ts`, only outside development
  and when both public PostHog configuration values are present.
- Capture events in feature handlers, once per executed action. Preserve event
  names and property shapes for existing actions. Keep analytics out of shared UI
  components.
- Record metadata such as query length, entity type, and result position rather
  than raw search text or response payloads.
- Use `posthogLogger` for frontend diagnostic logs. Keep client error capture in
  the existing hook instead of adding duplicate exception reports.

### Design system

- Read the [component reference](frontend/src/lib/ui/README.md) and
  [composition recipes](frontend/src/lib/ui/COMPOSITION.md) before adding UI.
  The interactive reference is `/design-system` in development only.
- Import components and types from `frontend/src/lib/ui/index.ts` through the
  appropriate relative path. Load `frontend/src/lib/ui/styles.css` once in the
  root layout.
- Reuse components and typed variants. Use tokens for colors, spacing, and
  focus. Purple identifies MPs, teal identifies funders, and utility icons use
  the muted neutral color.
- Keep page arrangement, URLs, async work, and financial formatting in features.
  Shared UI accepts presentation models. Scope feature CSS to page arrangement
  and caller-authored content rather than component internals.
- Extend reusable patterns in `frontend/src/lib/ui`. Export public additions
  from the barrel, document their contracts, and add a gallery example. Cover
  changed behavior in `frontend/tests/design-system.spec.ts` or feature tests.

### UI verification

- Run `npm run check`, `npm run build`, and the affected Playwright tests from
  `frontend`. Gallery tests use a development server. Production tests use the
  built application.
- Every PR that changes the UI must include desktop screenshots in its
  description. Capture the affected views from the running application on
  the PR branch after completing the changes.
- Upload screenshots as GitHub attachments with `gh pr create --attach` or
  `gh pr edit --attach`. Use a GitHub CLI version that supports this flag. Never
  commit PR screenshots to the repository. Verify that the attachments render
  in the PR description before marking the PR ready for review.


## Git history

- After completing and validating a task, commit its changes on the task's work
  branch, push the branch, and open a pull request against the target branch
  without waiting for a separate request. If the branch already has an open PR,
  update it instead of creating a duplicate.
- Before reporting completion, verify that the remote branch matches local
  `HEAD` and that the open PR targets the intended base and includes that commit.
  Include the PR URL and validation results in the final response.
- If pushing or opening the PR fails, report the blocker and the remaining step.
  Do not describe a local commit alone as completed delivery. Follow explicit
  user instructions to stop before pushing or opening a PR.
- Never commit directly on `main`.
- Keep Git history linear. Rebase feature branches onto the target branch and
  integrate changes with a fast-forward or squash; do not create merge commits.

| Rule | Enforcement |
| --- | --- |
| Deliver validated changes as a pushed branch with an open PR. | Agent completion check against the remote branch and `gh pr view`; include the verified PR URL in the final response. This is a workflow rule, not an automated gate. CI cannot observe work that was never pushed. |

## Development database migrations

- Keep schema changes in `db/migrations` as SQLx versioned `.up.sql` and
  `.down.sql` pairs. From the repository root, create a pair with
  `sqlx migrate add --source db/migrations --reversible <name>`.
- Never change a migration file that existed before the current PR. Treat those
  migrations as immutable, even when they have not been applied locally.
- When a PR's schema design changes, you must edit, consolidate, or remove the
  migrations introduced by that PR. Do not append a corrective migration for an
  obsolete step in the same PR. Before review, the PR must contain only the
  migrations needed for its final schema. Recreate isolated test databases that
  applied a discarded PR migration; do not preserve obsolete steps just to
  satisfy their checksums.
- Do not fold changes into the baseline or put manual schema scripts in
  `db/upgrades`.
- From the repository root, apply migrations with
  `sqlx migrate run --config sqlx.toml --source db/migrations`, inspect them with
  `sqlx migrate info --config sqlx.toml --source db/migrations`, and revert the
  latest version with
  `sqlx migrate revert --config sqlx.toml --source db/migrations`.
  Commands read the root `.env`; set `DATABASE_URL` to select another database.
- SQLx owns each migration transaction. Do not add `BEGIN` or `COMMIT` to the
  migration files. Keep each down migration limited to its up migration's changes.
- Test forward upgrades with existing records and the full down/up cycle in an
  isolated database. Preserve imported data when upgrading an existing database.
- The one-time transition from the consolidated baseline requires schema and
  data verification before aligning its checksum. Follow `db/README.md`;
  changing the checksum alone does not apply schema changes.

REGISTER OF MEMBERS' FINANCIAL INTERESTS 
Updates 3 – 30 September 2024 
 
 
The Register is maintained by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards. 
 
It is updated fortnightly online when Parliament is sitting, and less frequently at other times. 
 
MPs must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than 
earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election, 
and MPs must register any change in those registrable interests within 28 days. 
 
Interests remain on the Register for 12 months after their date of registration, most recent 
update or end date, whichever is later. 
 
This document contains only those interests added since the previous version of the Register. 
 
Entries in bold italics indicates interests that have been subject to an investigation by the 
Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards and subsequently rectified. 
 
Rectification decisions, together with the relevant evidence, are published on the 
Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards’ section of the Parliament website.  
 
For appointments registered under ‘Category 1: Employment and earnings’, MPs who ceased 
to hold Ministerial office within the previous two years are required to state whether they 
sought the advice of the Advisory Committee on Business Appointments (ACOBA). 
 
This document does not include minor corrections.

REGISTERING INTERESTS

The office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards, who oversees the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, sends all new MPs a registration form and a copy of the current rules of the House, and also arranges a personal briefing.

You must complete and return the form within one month of your election. After your initial register entry, you must notify the registry within four weeks of any changes to your registrable interests, subject to the financial thresholds.

DECLARING INTERESTS

Declaring interests is different to registering interests. Declaration means drawing attention to registered or unregistered interests on almost any occasion when someone else might consider them to influence what you say or do.

You are required to declare your interests, if relevant, from the time of your election, even before you’ve submitted an entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. You are expected to declare a wide range of interests. They include not just registered interests but

  * the interests of partners and family members
  * past interests up to one year old
  * expected future interests

You must declare interests not just when speaking but, for example, when submitting questions and early day motions, when requesting adjournment debates or emergency debates, when joining a select committee and when adding names to early day motions and other motions. In these circumstances an [R] will be included against your name when it appears on the Order Paper. But you’re not expected to declare an interest when asking an oral question or a supplementary question in the Chamber, or when it would unduly delay the business of the House.

MPS' STAFF INTERESTS

MPs' staff who hold a parliamentary pass sponsored by an MP are required to register outside employment and gifts, benefits and hospitality, subject to financial thresholds, in the Register of Members' Secretaries and Research Assistants.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Written evidence from the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards (OPCS) (GEP0005)

  1. The Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards (OPCS) welcomes the Committee’s inquiry.

 

  2. As the Committee’s Call for Evidence notes, t he 2024 General Election represented the highest number of new MPs elected at a General Election since 19 45.

 

  3. The Code of Conduct approved by the House requires: 

New Members must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election, and Members must register any change in those registrable interests within 28 days.[1]

 

  4. Each of the 350 MPs who had not been MPs in the previous Parliament were therefore required to complete their register of interest s by 4 August 2024, through the Registration Portal.

 

  5. Returning Members were required to review their entry in the last edition of the Register and submit any updates or changes to their registrable interests via the Registration Portal, or otherwise to confirm no updates or changes to their registrable interests (by email to the Registrations team, which is part of OPCS).

## 1

Registration of Members’ Financial Interests

### 

Requirements of the House

1. Paragraph 5 of the Code of Conduct for Members of Parliament provides:

Members must fulfil conscientiously the requirements of the House in respect of the registration of interests in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. New Members must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election, and Members must register any change in those registrable interests within 28 days.

2. The House therefore requires new Members, within one month of their election, to register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election. After that, Members are required to register within 28 days any change in those registrable interests. Such a change includes both the acquisition of a new interest and the ceasing of any registered interest, for example because an employment has ceased or because a holding has reduced in value or been sold.

The most likely explanation is **an initial registration deadline covering existing interests**, rather than a sudden surge in new financial activity.

After the election:

- **350 new MPs had to register by 4 August 2024.** This included all current financial interests and registrable benefits other than earnings received during the previous 12 months.
- **Returning MPs had to review their existing entries** and submit changes or confirm that nothing had changed.

The Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards confirms both requirements in its [evidence about the 2024 election](https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/161194/html/).

That deadline falls on the final day of our busiest week, **29 July to 4 August**, when 2,605 declarations were registered. The timing strongly supports an initial-registration explanation, although we haven’t classified each entry individually.

So the graph starts with MPs recording a **stock of existing interests**. Later months mostly capture changes and new interests. Registration dates therefore shouldn’t be read as the dates when money was received.

Written questions, answers and statements

### Question

Mr Richard Holden Conservative Basildon and Billericay Commons

To ask the hon. Member for Blaenau Gwent and Rhymney, representing the House of Commons Commission, what guidance the House of Commons issues to hon. Members on declaring reportable gifts, donations or hospitality which are returned or reimbursed within 28 days of receipt; and whether reportable gifts, donations or hospitality which are returned or reimbursed after 28 days of receipt are recorded in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests.

### Answer

Nick Smith Labour Blaenau Gwent and Rhymney Commons

### Answered on

21 January 2025

Registration requirements are set out in the Code of Conduct together with the Guide to the Rules relating to the Conduct of Members, approved by the House on 12 December 2022. (https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5803/cmcode/1083/1083.pdf)

Paragraph 5 of the Code provides that new Members must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election, and Members must register any change in those registrable interests within 28 days. Gifts, donations or hospitality are registrable from the day of receipt (whether or not subsequently repaid). The 28-day period is provided to enable time for registration for the purpose of transparency.

Members are encouraged to seek advice from the Registrar of Members’ Financial Interests if they are in any doubt about whether a proposed course of action is in line with the rules.

House of Commons Commission

**Potentially, but the initial spike alone doesn’t establish double counting.** There are two different cases.

**The same declaration appearing in successive registers is counted once.** The importer selects its latest published version, updates the existing declaration by Parliament’s ID, and replaces its funding entries. It doesn’t add another copy each time the register is published. [Version selection](/Users/jamie/development/exposed/exposed/src/lib/outbound/declaration_source.rs:179), [database loading](/Users/jamie/development/exposed/exposed/src/lib/outbound/declaration_loading.rs:824).

**The same underlying payment recorded under two different declaration IDs could be counted twice.** The importer treats those as separate declarations. I haven’t established whether that happens across the election boundary.

There’s also a separate timing issue. An interest registered in July 2024 can describe a benefit received before the election. It enters our current-term totals because those use **registration dates**, even if the benefit itself predates this Parliament.

Returning MPs were required to review and update their existing entries, so we shouldn’t assume they all registered everything again. [Parliament’s guidance](https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/161194/html/).

The supported conclusion is that **repeated publication is handled, but duplicate underlying payments across different IDs remain unverified**. Our totals describe declared records, rather than a deduplicated ledger of money received.
